title: Build a reply sorter for your outbound inbox
description: A system that reads replies to your outbound sequences, sorts each into a category, and recommends the next action.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

action.title: Action
action.content: A step an automation performs after the trigger fires — like 'send a Slack message' or 'create a Notion page.' One workflow can chain a dozen actions off a single trigger.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

context.title: Context
context.content: Everything Claude can 'see' in a given session — your messages, files you've shared, instructions, and conversation history. The more relevant context you give Claude, the better its output.

hubspot.title: HubSpot
hubspot.content: A CRM and marketing platform used by sales, marketing, and customer success teams. Common target for AI automations — students connect it to draft outreach, enrich contacts, or sync data with other tools.

batch-api.title: Batch API
batch-api.content: A way to send a big pile of requests to Claude at once and get the results back later (usually within 24 hours) at a discount. Good for one-time bulk jobs like classifying 10,000 customer support tickets.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Personalized, signal-based outreach already pulls in more replies than generic templates, per [Autobound's Cold Email Guide](https://www.autobound.ai/blog/cold-email-guide-2026). That extra volume turns into an unmanaged inbox fast unless something sorts it first. A misclassified "not interested" can bury a real objection, and an unsubscribe or wrong-contact reply left unsorted carries compliance exposure under CAN-SPAM and GDPR opt-out rules.

This system reads every reply to your outbound sequences and sorts it into a category (interested, objection, referral, unsubscribe, wrong contact, not now, out of office), then recommends a next action for each, so a full inbox gets triaged in minutes.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) each time you clear your inbox, a saved skill, or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that watches for new replies and flags what needs you. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) until you approve a send or a CRM change.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your categories, where replies land, the next action per category, and whether the system drafts responses or only recommends.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that reads replies to my outbound emails and sorts each into a category with a recommended next step. Ask me questions, one at a time, about which categories matter, where replies land, what a next action looks like per category, and whether the system should draft responses or just recommend. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming the categories and next [actions](#tooltip-action) up front keeps the sorter consistent instead of inventing new labels every run.

items: Who owns the suppression list and how fast an unsubscribe must reach it.
Which categories need a drafted response versus a flag.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are your email inbox (Gmail, Outlook), your sequencing tool (Outreach, Salesloft, Instantly), and your CRM (Salesforce, [HubSpot](#tooltip-hubspot)). The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on a real reply. The prompt below is an example of the core task. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Classify the attached reply from [contact] and recommend a next action.

Context: Categories are interested, objection, referral, unsubscribe, wrong contact, not now, out of office; next actions per category are [describe].

Rules: One category per reply; if ambiguous, say so and explain why; treat opt-out language as immediate; never send a drafted response without review.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: forcing a stated reason on ambiguous replies stops the sorter from guessing silently and mislabeling something that needs a person's attention.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. One category per reply, ambiguous cases explained, opt-outs treated as immediate?
**Feedback.** Correct the rules that produced the wrong call. Don't just fix the label on that one reply.

items: Auto-update the CRM stage on clear interest.
Route referrals to the right rep.
Flag repeat "not now" replies for nurture.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Skip the feel check. Have your AI chat draft rubric and run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each reply classification, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, replies classified, categories confirmed correct, misclassifications, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a recurring misclassification visible after a [batch](#tooltip-batch-api) or two.

children.text: **Log** every batch against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. After a couple weeks it shows which categories keep getting misrouted and which next actions never fire as written. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a few weeks straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults instead of a blank chat. When the log shows the same check failing again and again, that gap is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. Treating every category as equally low-stakes misses that opt-outs carry compliance risk while objections carry revenue risk, so give it that weight every run.
